newsitem.title: UK: Sterling holds gains on mark after rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Sterling holds gains on mark after rate rise.

text.p: Sterling acclaimed Gordon Brown's first moves as Chancellor by rallying three pfennigs and one cent, but the feeling was that once the dust settles the outlook is for an easier pound.
As the market had expected, Brown fell in line with long standing calls from the Bank of England for a quarter-point inflation-dampening rise in six percent base lending rates.
But it was the news that the Bank of England was to be given independence in setting interest rates that really caught the market's attention and sterling advanced strongly.
Setting monetary policy independent of political interference would appear to be bullish for the pound in the long term.

But with exporters already struggling the last thing the new administration needs is a still stronger pound. Forex traders latched on to Brown's phrase that he wanted a "...stable and competitive pound over the medium term..."
"The key here is the phrase 'stable and competitive'," said Nick Parsons, foreign exchange strategist at Banque Paribas.
"The use of the word 'competitive' has to rule out a pound much higher from where we are now."

Sticking to the dictum "Buy the rumour, sell the fact", the market initially pushed the pound lower after the rate rise news. But sterling subsequently picked up to 2.8300 marks compared with the 2.80 it was trading at just ahead of the news, it's highest level since August 1992.

"Background comments from the new chancellor suggest some concern about the pound's strength and this was almost certainly a reason whey the hike was kept to 25 basis points," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica.
"Apparent commitment to keep control over the pound is likely to make additional gains harder to come by."
While the devaluation stain has never completely left Labour, analysts said the days when the party needed a strong pound to boost credibility have long since passed.
In fact, a lower pound would be seen as a success for Brown in rebalancing the economy.
It would be difficult for the new administration to directly influence the level of the pound now that there is a feeling that the interest rate plateau has been brought forward.
This and an expected tightening in fiscal policy in the next budget -- Brown has said he will hold one within two months -- will weigh on the economy, and therefore the pound, further out.
"Near-term, we could be heading up to 2.85 against the mark. Longer-term, the economic fundamentals suggest it could be weaker," said Adrian Owen, International Economist at Julius Baer Investments.
"It is bad news for the government and this is, partly, why I think we will see a weaker pound by year-end. The obvious answer is tighter fiscal policy." he added.
Bank of England independence also raises the question of Britain's participation in European monetary union (EMU), although the ERM criteria has yet to be met.
A country's currency belong to the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) for two years before it can join EMU.

"BOE independence leaves the door wide open for EMU participation but you have to think about the ERM implications and what the right level for sterling is," said Ian Amstad, International Economist at Bankers Trust.
"And we are clearly above the right level now. This may be short-term bullish for the pound bit it reinforces the view that in the medium to longer term it will come back down again."
